prompt: A Service has four pods. kube-proxy's iptables rules give the first rule a probability of 0.25. What probability does the second rule carry?
hint: Each rule shares out what the rules before it left.

choices.text: 0.25, the same as the first
choices.why: Then the second pod would get a quarter of three quarters, less than its share.

choices.text: One in three
choices.why: Right. Three pods remain for what is left, and the third rule then carries 0.5.

choices.text: 0.5, as in the capture
choices.why: 0.5 was the second rule with three pods in all.

choices.text: 0.75, what the first left over
choices.why: That is what reaches the second rule, not the share it takes.

prompt: A gRPC client keeps one connection open to a Service with three pods. One pod is busy and the other two are idle. Why?

choices.text: The busy pod has the lowest IP address
choices.why: The order of the rules does not change anybody's share.

choices.text: Session affinity is on by default
choices.why: The default is `None`.

choices.text: The pod was drawn once, at connect
choices.why: Right. The draw is per connection, and every request since went down that one.

choices.text: kube-proxy sends more to faster pods
choices.why: It knows nothing about how busy a pod is.

prompt: Three hundred requests split 96, 91 and 113 across three pods. What does that show?
hint: An exact share would be 100 each.

choices.text: The third pod answers faster than the others
choices.why: Speed plays no part in the draw.

choices.text: Random is fair on average, not per hundred
choices.why: Right. The shares converge over many connections.

choices.text: One of the three rules is misconfigured
choices.why: The probabilities were exactly one third, one half and the rest.

choices.text: Affinity was on
choices.why: With affinity on, all 300 went to one pod.

prompt: A team turns on `sessionAffinity: ClientIP` so that logged-in users keep their session. Their users reach the cluster through one corporate gateway. What happens?
hint: What address does each user arrive from?

choices.text: Each user keeps their own pod
choices.why: They all share one address, so they share one pod.

choices.text: Everybody lands on one pod
choices.why: Right. Affinity keys on the address, and the gateway gives them all the same one.

choices.text: The Service refuses ClientIP behind a gateway
choices.why: Nothing checks where addresses come from.

choices.text: Sessions now survive a pod's deletion
choices.why: Affinity ends with the pod, and so does what it held in memory.

prompt: Under `externalTrafficPolicy: Cluster`, the shop's log showed `172.18.0.7` for a request the laptop sent. Why not the laptop's address?
hint: The answer has to come back the same way.

choices.text: The node rewrote the source address
choices.why: Right. The reply has to come back through the node that forwarded it, and the address is what that costs.

choices.text: The laptop has that address
choices.why: The laptop was 172.18.0.1; .7 was the control-plane node.

choices.text: curl hides the source address it sends
choices.why: Under `Local` the same curl showed the laptop's address.

choices.text: The shop logs only the addresses of nodes
choices.why: It logs whatever source arrived; under `Local` that was the laptop.

prompt: Under `externalTrafficPolicy: Local`, a request reaches a node that runs none of the Service's pods. What happens?

choices.text: It is forwarded to a node with a pod
choices.why: That is `Cluster`.

choices.text: kube-proxy starts a pod on that node
choices.why: kube-proxy only writes rules; it never starts pods.

choices.text: No answer
choices.why: Right. Two of the three nodes answered nothing.

choices.text: It gets a 503 from the Service
choices.why: A Service sends no HTTP answers of its own.

prompt: A Service uses `externalTrafficPolicy: Local` behind a cloud load balancer. How does the load balancer avoid the nodes without a pod?
hint: Kubernetes gives such a Service something extra.

choices.text: It sends to every node and retries on failure
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson retries; the nodes are filtered before traffic is sent.

choices.text: A health check that only pod nodes pass
choices.why: Right. Each node answers the check with success only while it runs a pod, and traffic goes to the nodes that pass.

choices.text: The cloud reads the pod list from etcd
choices.why: No load balancer reads etcd.

choices.text: It cannot; Local only works with NodePort
choices.why: `Local` was designed for exactly this case.

prompt: Match each setting with what it decides.
hint: Two were in the first section, one in the second.

pairs.right: The same client goes to the same pod
Only pods on the receiving node serve
Any node may forward to any pod

right_distractors: Requests go to the least busy pod

prompt: With `externalTrafficPolicy: Local`, a load balancer splits traffic evenly between two nodes. Node A runs one pod of the Service and node B runs three. What percentage of the traffic does the pod on node A receive?
hint: Half goes to each node; the node splits its half among its own pods.

prompt: To let the application see the caller's real address, set the Service's `externalTrafficPolicy` to ___.
hint: The one where two nodes gave no answer.
